data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    size = max(1, min(n, 20))
    nums = [rng.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(size)]
    return [nums]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    size = max(1, min(n, 20))
    nums = list(range(size, 0, -1))
    return [nums]

data.key_insight: Maintain an array tails where tails[i] stores the smallest tail of all increasing subsequences of length i+1. Using binary search, we can efficiently update tails as we iterate through the array.

steps.title: Initialize tails array
steps.detail: Create an empty list 'tails' to store the smallest tail for each subsequence length.

steps.title: Iterate through numbers
steps.detail: For each number in nums, use binary search to find its insertion position in tails.

steps.title: Update tails
steps.detail: If the number is larger than all elements in tails, append it. Otherwise, replace the element at the found insertion index.

steps.title: Return length
steps.detail: The length of tails at the end of the iteration is the length of the longest increasing subsequence.

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic programming breaks a problem down into overlapping subproblems, storing results to avoid recomputing them. Reach for it when finding optimal arrangements or subsequences where choices at one step depend on previous steps.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The longest increasing subsequence ending at any index can be derived from the longest increasing subsequences of the indices that come before it.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers work well for contiguous subarrays or sorted arrays with opposite ends moving inward, but subsequences do not need to be contiguous here.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding windows are used for contiguous subarrays of a given size or condition, whereas subsequences can skip elements.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Simply picking the next larger element locally does not guarantee the longest overall subsequence.

signals.hint: Points to finding an optimal sequence by picking elements in order without requiring them to be next to each other.

signals.phrase: does not need to be contiguous
signals.hint: Confirms we can skip elements, ruling out standard contiguous subarray techniques.

data.brute_force_idea: Generate every possible subset of the input array, check if each subset is strictly increasing, and track the maximum length found among those that are.
data.brute_force_why: There are 2^n possible subsets, and for each subset, we spend O(n) time to check if it is strictly increasing and to measure its length.
data.bottleneck: Generating all 2^n subsets tests many redundant or invalid combinations, re-checking overlapping subsequences from scratch every time.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many subsets are generated as the length of the input increases.
Notice that many subsets share common prefixes that get re-evaluated repeatedly.
Ask whether you need to test every single subset or if you can build longer valid sequences from shorter ones already solved.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach checks all subsets in exponential time by generating every combination. The optimized approach maintains an array tails where each element is the smallest tail of all increasing subsequences of a given length found so far. By using binary search to find the correct placement for each number in nums, we avoid scanning previous subsequences entirely.

derivation.note: The loop iterates through each of the n elements in nums.
Performs a binary search on the tails array of length at most n.
Appends to the tails array when a larger element extends the LIS.
Updates an existing tail element in place.

data.time_summary: Line 4 runs n times, and inside the loop, line 5 executes a binary search costing O(log n). The other operations inside the loop run in O(1) time. Multiplying the loop count by the search cost yields O(n log n) total time, which matches the measured evidence where step counts scale linearly-logarithmically rather than exponentially.
data.space_summary: The extra memory is used by the tails array, which stores at most one element per input item in the worst case, resulting in O(n) space complexity.
data.takeaway: When building a sequence where only the smallest ending elements matter for future extensions, maintain a dynamic tracking array and use binary search to place incoming elements.
mistakes: Treating tails as the actual longest increasing subsequence instead of just an array of ending values.
Using a linear scan instead of bisect_left, which would degrade the time complexity back to O(n^2).
Forgetting to handle the case where the new element is smaller than all existing tails, which incorrectly appends instead of replacing.

events.label: Tutor: build the visual explanation

data.overview: The Longest Increasing Subsequence algorithm uses patience sorting and binary search to build a dynamic array of smallest ending values for increasing subsequences of various lengths. As we process each number, we use binary search to either extend our longest subsequence or improve an existing smaller tail.
data.intuition: Imagine organizing a deck of cards into piles according to patience sorting rules: each new card goes on top of the leftmost pile whose top card is greater than or equal to it. The number of piles at the end represents the length of the longest increasing subsequence.

pitfalls: Mistaking the tails array for the actual longest increasing subsequence itself; tails only tracks the minimum end values.
Using standard linear search instead of binary search, which degrades the time complexity from O(N log N) to O(N^2).
Failing to handle strictly increasing constraints correctly by using bisect_right instead of bisect_left.
